claims.text: Tungsten-based HEA intermediate layers are currently used in plasma-facing reactor components.
The proposed intervention is to add approximately 5–10 wt.% copper to a tungsten-based HEA during synthesis.
Adding 5–10 wt.% copper will improve the heat-transfer capability of tungsten-based HEA intermediate layers.
Copper addition will not compromise the mechanical strength of the tungsten-based HEA.
Copper addition will not compromise the radiation resistance of the tungsten-based HEA.
Plasma-facing materials experience extreme heat and intense particle fluxes.
Plasma-facing materials must withstand neutron irradiation and helium and hydrogen fluxes.
The proposed benefit should hold at surface temperatures approaching 1000°C.
Copper atoms will be homogeneously dispersed within the HEA matrix.
Dispersed copper atoms will form enhanced electron-conduction pathways.
Copper will integrate into the solid-solution lattice while maintaining grain stability.
Copper incorporation will increase the alloy's free-electron density.
The increase in free-electron density will improve thermal conductivity.
High-entropy and solid-solution effects will preserve mechanical robustness under reactor conditions.
High-entropy and solid-solution effects will preserve radiation resistance under reactor conditions.
Copper-doped samples will have higher thermal conductivity than undoped tungsten-based HEA samples.
The mechanical strength of copper-doped samples will remain comparable to or slightly exceed that of the undoped baseline.
Resistance to irradiation-induced damage in copper-doped samples will remain comparable to or slightly exceed that of the undoped baseline.
Operation outside the proposed temperature and loading regime may reduce the conduction benefit or cause microstructural instability.
Higher copper concentrations may cause phase separation or embrittlement.
